Free anxiety tools

20 short exercises on anxiety, 2 to 8 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • Where anxiety shows up in your body

    Choose the physical sensations you notice when you feel anxious. Most people are surprised how many of them they had stopped counting.

    Card pick · 4 min

  • What unsettles you, and how much

    Sort everyday situations by how often they leave you on edge. The point is the pattern across them, not any single one.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • How anxiety tends to operate in you

    Rate how often a set of common anxious habits has been true for you lately. You will see which show up most and which barely feature.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Avoid or approach

    Place things you have been avoiding on a grid of how much you avoid them against how much they matter to you.

    Grid · 6 min

  • The anatomy of one anxious moment

    Walk back through a recent spike of anxiety step by step: what led up to it, what you felt, what you did, and what happened next.

    Guided writing · 8 min

  • Box breathing

    Four seconds in, four held, four out, four held. A steady square of breath many people use to settle a keyed-up body.

    Breathing · 3 min

  • Build your steadying kit

    Assemble a personal list of things that help you feel more grounded: senses, people, places, phrases, and small actions.

    Plan builder · 6 min

  • When anxiety peaks across your week

    Mark the times of day and days of the week when anxiety tends to be loudest. A shape usually appears.

    Week map · 3 min

  • Anxiety on seven dials

    Set a dial for each way anxiety can take up room: how loud it is in your body, how much it steers your choices, how long it lingers. The spread across the dials says more than any single one.

    Dials · 4 min

  • The little things you do to feel safe

    Tick the small precautions you have picked up to keep anxiety at bay. They are so ordinary that most people never think of them as anxiety at all.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Dread in the morning, the day as it was

    Each morning, rate how much you are dreading the day. Each evening, rate how hard it actually turned out to be. After a week, the gap between the two lines is the point.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • Which kind of anxious

    Anxious is a wide word. Narrow it to the flavor you are actually feeling, find where it sits in your body, and hear what it might be asking for.

    Feelings wheel · 3 min

  • The smoke alarm check

    Treat a wave of anxiety like a smoke alarm going off: check for actual smoke, thank the alarm, and give it two minutes to quiet down. A short exercise for the moment it hits.

    Guided exercise · 6 min

  • What anxiety asks for, and what else you could give it

    Turn over cards that show a demand anxiety makes on one side and a smaller, kinder alternative on the other. Keep the ones you could imagine trying.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • What you reach for first

    Rank the things you reach for when anxiety rises, from the one you grab first to the one you get to last. The order shows your reflexes, which is different from what you would choose.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • What an anxious hour is made of

    Think of a typical stretch of feeling anxious and divide 100 points across what your mind was actually doing in it. Anxious time is a mix, and the mix is the useful part.

    Budget · 4 min

  • The rules anxiety wrote for you

    Choose the unspoken rules you find yourself living by to keep anxiety quiet, then put them in order of how tightly you keep them. Seeing them written down is often the first time they look like rules.

    Card pick · 5 min

  • A time it went better than you feared

    Write about one thing you dreaded that turned out fine, or at least survivable. Anxiety keeps careful records of disasters and almost none of the near misses; this evens the books a little.

    Guided writing · 8 min

  • When anxiety is on your side

    Sort things anxiety makes you do into the ones that genuinely serve you, the ones that get in your way, and the ones that do both. Not every anxious habit needs to go.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • How likely, and how bad

    Place the outcomes you fear on a grid of how likely they really are against how bad they would be if they happened. Anxiety tends to put everything in one corner.

    Grid · 6 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
